claims.text: The onset and progression of the premelting and melting transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by localized elemental segregation driven by differential thermal expansion.
Localized segregation creates compositional inhomogeneities that locally lower the melting point.
Regions with locally depressed melting points act as specific nucleation sites for the phase transition.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and compositionally homogeneous.
A minor homogenizing dopant can suppress segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Nanoscale segregated regions form preferentially at grain boundaries or defect sites.
Differential thermal expansion among the constituent elements causes local strain as the nanoparticles approach melting.
Thermally induced local strain facilitates atomic migration and elemental segregation.
Segregated regions have reduced cohesive energy.
Reduced cohesive energy in segregated regions depresses their local melting temperature.
Early-stage melting will be spatially localized in regions showing elemental inhomogeneity.
Nanoparticles in which segregation is suppressed will initiate melting at a higher temperature than untreated nanoparticles.
The room-temperature baseline nanoparticles lack preexisting compositional gradients.
The proposed mechanism applies just below and into the melting regime under inert conditions, with oxidation and external mechanical stress excluded.
Post-synthesis annealing can be used as an alternative to doping to reduce local compositional fluctuations.
If segregation-suppressed and untreated nanoparticles have the same melting-onset temperature and spatial melting pattern, the proposed segregation mechanism is falsified.
